Starting from the theme of innovation in fabrication, our team focused on simplifying joints and fasteners. A single wire ratchet gear became the core fastener: wire tension secures the parts, simplifying assembly while shaping a clean furniture system.

I designed and developed the stool in the WRG series, considering loads and force directions in its structure. Three outward-splayed legs support the seat; under load, the joints between the seat and legs are intended to engage more firmly. Wire tension and T-shaped welded reinforcement work together to support the structure and limit deformation of the steel plates.
36:553: The stool is built around a wire ratchet gear fastener. Sketching and modeling developed the seat-to-leg joints, the direction in which the legs spread and the tension of the wire as one structural system.
36:615: I selected stainless steel for its corrosion resistance, durability and welding requirements, with a hairline finish. Fabrication specifications defined thickness, bends, weld positions and assembly offsets. This experience later led me to learn and practice welding myself.

The Aviator is a kinetic speaker whose wings change the position and orientation of two full-range drivers. The drivers face upward when folded and turn toward the listener as the wings open, offering two listening arrangements within one object.

The folded configuration is intended to distribute sound through the space without a fixed listening position. Opening the wings increases the distance between the drivers and turns them toward the user. This visible transformation makes the change in listening mode easy to understand.
54:928: The form exposes the joints, links and wires that produce movement. Their connections and operation shape the object, giving the opening wings a functional purpose. The Aviator connects mechanical movement with listening intent, showing where sound is directed through its form.
